title: Indus Valley Civilization
summary: The Indus Valley Civilization was one of the world's earliest urban cultures, flourishing in the Indus River basin from about 3300 to 1300 BCE, with planned cities, standardised weights, and a script that remains undeciphered.

rows.label: Discovered

intro: The Indus Valley Civilization, also known as the Harappan Civilization, was one of the world's earliest urban cultures and one of its greatest. Flourishing in the Indus River basin of modern Pakistan and northwest India from about 3300 to 1300 BCE, it built cities of a scale and sophistication unmatched in the ancient world: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, each with populations in the tens of thousands, laid out on grids, served by covered drains, and supplied with water from hundreds of wells. Its people traded with Mesopotamia, standardised their weights and measures across a million square kilometres, and wrote in a script that no one has yet deciphered.

The civilization was lost to history for four thousand years. Its cities were abandoned, its script forgotten, and its very existence unknown until the 1920s, when archaeologists of the Archaeological Survey of India excavated Mohenjo-daro and Harappa and recognised a civilisation that had rivalled Mesopotamia and Egypt. The discovery was one of the great archaeological revelations of the twentieth century, and it rewrote the history of South Asia, revealing an urban tradition that predates the Vedic period and the arrival of Indo-Aryan languages.

The Indus Valley Civilization remains a mystery in its essentials. Its people left no palaces, no royal tombs, and no deciphered texts; its religion, its political organisation, and its language are all matters of inference. What survives is the evidence of its cities: their planning, their engineering, their craft, and their commerce. That evidence testifies to a civilisation of remarkable achievement, whose legacy — in urban planning, in craft, and in the cultural heritage of South Asia — endures to this day.

sections.heading: The River and the Land
paragraphs: The Indus Valley Civilization was a product of its geography. The Indus River, rising in Tibet and flowing through the Himalayan foothills to the Arabian Sea, floods annually, depositing fertile silt across its floodplain. The monsoon rains water the region, and the alluvial soils support agriculture on a scale that can feed cities. The civilization occupied a territory of more than a million square kilometres, from the Makran coast in the west to the Ganges plain in the east, and from the Himalayan foothills in the north to the sea in the south. It was the largest of the ancient world's civilisations by area. The floods that fertilised its fields were governed by the same celestial mechanics that order the solar system.

The land offered both abundance and danger. The floods that fertilised the fields also destroyed settlements, and the cities were built on raised platforms of mud brick to withstand inundation. The rivers provided transport and trade, linking the interior to the sea and to Mesopotamia beyond. The hills on the civilization's margins provided timber, stone, and minerals, while the plains provided grain, cotton, and livestock. The civilization's economy was a river economy, and its cities were nodes in a network of water and land routes.

The civilization's relationship with its environment was sustainable for two thousand years. Its farmers grew wheat, barley, cotton, and millets; its herders raised cattle, sheep, and goats; and its craftsmen worked in stone, metal, ivory, and shell. The scale of its agriculture supported its cities without the irrigation bureaucracies of Mesopotamia or the flood management of Egypt. The Indus Valley was a land of plenty, and its civilisation was built on that plenty.

sections.heading: The Great Cities: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa
paragraphs: Mohenjo-daro, whose name means the Mound of the Dead in Sindhi, was the largest city of the civilization, covering some two hundred and fifty hectares and housing perhaps forty thousand people. Its streets were laid out on a grid, oriented to the cardinal directions, and its houses were built of standardised fired bricks in the ratio of one to two to four. The city possessed a Great Bath, a watertight pool of baked brick that was probably used for ritual bathing, and a network of covered drains that carried waste from the houses to the streets. No other ancient city, in Mesopotamia or Egypt, matched its sanitation.

Harappa, the second great city, gave the civilisation its alternative name. It was a planned city of similar sophistication, with a citadel mound, a grid of streets, and workshops that produced the civilisation's characteristic seals, weights, and tools. Dholavira, in Gujarat, was divided into three walled towns and possessed elaborate water reservoirs that harvested the monsoon rains. Lothal, on the Gulf of Khambhat, was a port and manufacturing centre whose dockyard is among the earliest in the world. Each city was distinct, but all shared the civilisation's standards of planning and craft.

The cities' uniformity is their most striking feature. Bricks were made to a standard ratio across the entire civilisation; weights followed a precise binary and decimal system; and seals were carved to a common style. This uniformity suggests a civilisation with strong central coordination, whether through a state, a merchant network, or a shared cultural authority. Yet no palace or temple has been identified, and no king's tomb has been found. The Indus Valley Civilization achieved urban sophistication without the visible apparatus of kingship that marks the other ancient civilisations.

sections.heading: Trade, Weights, and the Mesopotamian Connection
paragraphs: The Indus Valley Civilization was a trading civilisation. Its merchants exported cotton, ivory, timber, carnelian beads, and exotic animals to Mesopotamia, where cuneiform texts record the arrival of goods from Meluhha, the Mesopotamian name for the Indus region. Indus seals have been found in Bahrain, Oman, and Iraq, and Mesopotamian seals in the Indus cities, testifying to a trade network that spanned the Arabian Sea. The civilisation's ports, caravans, and river boats carried its goods across a world that stretched from Central Asia to the Persian Gulf.

Trade depended on standardisation. The civilisation's weights, made of chert and following a precise system, were used from the Gulf to the Ganges, ensuring that goods could be measured and exchanged fairly across the entire region. The weights' accuracy — some are precise to within a fraction of a percent — testifies to a sophisticated metrology and a commercial culture of trust. The seals, carved with animals and inscriptions, served as signatures and guarantees of ownership, the ancient equivalent of trademarks. Such precision anticipates the standardised measurement that underpins the history of computing.

The trade with Mesopotamia declined after about 1900 BCE, as the Mesopotamian world changed and the sea routes shifted. The civilisation's cities continued, but their external commerce contracted. The decline of trade was one of several pressures that would eventually transform the civilisation, and it illustrates how deeply the Indus Valley was integrated into the ancient world's economy. The civilisation was not isolated; it was a partner in the first global trading system, and its fate was bound to that system's fate.

sections.heading: The Undeciphered Script
paragraphs: The Indus Valley Civilization wrote in a script of about four hundred signs, found on seals, pottery, and copper tablets. The inscriptions are short — the longest contains fewer than thirty signs — and no bilingual text, no Rosetta Stone, has been found to unlock them. The script remains undeciphered, and its language is unknown: it may have been Dravidian, Indo-Aryan, or a language unrelated to either. The undeciphered script is the civilisation's most tantalising mystery, the key to its texts that no one can read.

Attempts at decipherment have followed the paths that succeeded for other scripts. The signs have been analysed statistically, compared with known scripts, and interpreted as logographic, syllabic, and alphabetic systems. None has produced a convincing reading. The brevity of the inscriptions, the absence of a bilingual key, and the uncertainty about the underlying language make the Indus script exceptionally difficult. Some scholars argue that the signs are not writing at all but symbols of ownership and ritual; others insist that they encode a full language. The debate continues.

The script's mystery is a reminder of the fragility of knowledge. The civilisation that built Mohenjo-daro wrote, but its writing died with it, and four thousand years later its words are shapes without meaning. The fate of the Indus script parallels that of the Library of Alexandria: in both cases, a civilisation's records were lost, and in both cases, the loss impoverishes humanity's understanding of the past. The undeciphered seals are the Indus Valley's silent library. The recovery of lost writing would have to wait for the printing press, which made texts reproducible and therefore durable.

sections.heading: Religion, Art, and Daily Life
paragraphs: The religion of the Indus Valley Civilization must be inferred from its art and its remains. Seals depict a horned figure seated in a yogic posture, surrounded by animals, whom scholars have identified as a prototype of Shiva, the great god of later Hinduism. Other seals show a mother goddess, sacred trees, and ritual scenes. The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro suggests ritual bathing, and the civilisation's burials, though simple, indicate beliefs about an afterlife. The Indus religion appears to be an ancestor of the Hindu traditions that followed it, though the connections are debated.

The civilisation's art is remarkable for its naturalism and its craft. The bronze Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro, a nude figure with a confident stride, is a masterpiece of lost-wax casting. The Priest King, a bearded figure in a trefoil-patterned robe, is carved in steatite with extraordinary skill. The seals, with their animals and inscriptions, are miniature works of art. The civilisation's craftsmen worked in bronze, stone, ivory, shell, and faience, and their products — beads, bangles, seals, and tools — are found across the region. The Indus Valley was a civilisation of artisans as much as of farmers. The bronze and faience of its craftsmen obey the same quantum mechanics that governs every atom in the modern world.

Daily life in the Indus cities was comfortable by ancient standards. Houses had bathrooms, wells were everywhere, and the drains carried waste away from the streets. The diet included wheat, barley, millet, pulses, and meat, and the people wore cotton, which the civilisation pioneered. Games, toys, and jewellery testify to leisure and adornment. The civilisation's egalitarian character — its lack of palaces and royal tombs — suggests a society in which wealth was distributed more evenly than in the kingdoms of Mesopotamia and Egypt. The Indus Valley may have been the ancient world's most democratic urban culture.

sections.heading: Decline and Legacy
paragraphs: The Indus Valley Civilization declined after about 1900 BCE, and by 1300 BCE its cities were largely abandoned. The causes were multiple: the monsoon weakened, the rivers shifted, trade with Mesopotamia contracted, and the cities' water systems failed. The decline was gradual, not catastrophic: the population dispersed into smaller settlements, farming continued, and the civilisation's traditions persisted in the villages of the region. The great cities emptied, but the civilisation did not vanish; it transformed.

The legacy of the Indus Valley Civilization is visible in the cultural heritage of South Asia. Its urban planning, its craft traditions, its religious symbols, and its agricultural practices flowed into the societies that followed, including the Vedic and later Hindu cultures. The civilisation's cities, rediscovered in the twentieth century, are now UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and their excavation continues to reveal new information. The Indus Valley is the foundation of South Asian civilisation, and its study is essential to understanding the region's history. Today its cities are documented on the World Wide Web, where open archives preserve the evidence of its achievement.

The Indus Valley Civilization also stands as a monument to what civilisations can achieve. Without kings, without palaces, and without deciphered texts, its people built the most sophisticated cities of the ancient world, standardised their commerce across a million square kilometres, traded with Mesopotamia, and produced art of lasting beauty. Their civilisation was lost, but its cities remain, testifying to a world of achievement that history nearly forgot — and that archaeology has restored to memory. The same human curiosity that raised the Great Bath would, four thousand years later, measure the curvature of spacetime in the work of Albert Einstein and his general relativity, and the same sky that watched over Mohenjo-daro now reveals black holes at the centres of galaxies.
